calibration.instructions: Mark each statement True or False, then say how confident you are. 50% means you are guessing. 100% means you are certain. There is no penalty for saying you are unsure - we are checking whether your confidence matches your accuracy, not how much you know.

items.statement: The Pacific Ocean covers more area than all of Earth's land combined.
items.derivation: Pacific approx 165.2M km2; total land approx 148.9M km2.

items.statement: The Great Wall of China is visible to the naked eye from the Moon.
items.derivation: Not visible. The wall is metres wide; the Moon is approx 384,000 km away.

items.statement: Nitrogen makes up more of Earth's atmosphere than oxygen does.
items.derivation: Nitrogen approx 78 percent, oxygen approx 21 percent.

items.statement: A standard deck of cards has more face cards than the English alphabet has letters.
items.derivation: 12 face cards, 26 letters.

items.statement: The summit of Mount Everest is the point on Earth's surface farthest from the planet's centre.
items.derivation: Chimborazo's summit is farther from the centre because Earth bulges at the equator.

items.statement: Sound travels faster through water than through air.
items.derivation: Approx 1,480 m/s in water vs approx 343 m/s in air.

items.statement: Australia is wider from east to west than the Moon is across.
items.derivation: Australia approx 4,000 km east-west; Moon diameter approx 3,475 km.

items.statement: Old window glass is thicker at the bottom because glass slowly flows downward over centuries.
items.derivation: A myth. The thickness is an artefact of crown glass manufacture; glass does not flow measurably at room temperature.

scoring.note: gap = mean(confidence)/100 - (n_correct/n_items). Scored as ONE unit toward U.

options.text: Act now. 60% chance of a $30,000 gain, 40% chance of an $8,000 loss.
Wait three months for a change in probabilities. Gain becomes 75% and loss becomes 25%. Waiting reduces the gain to $16,000; the loss becomes $3,000.
Decline. $0.

items.stem: In which of these would the single largest event over ten years account for more than half of the ten-year total?

options.text: The combined weight of all packages shipped from one depot
Total insurance payouts for storm damage in a region
Total hours worked by a ten-person team
The combined height of everyone who walks through a train station

items.derivation: A, C and D are bounded and additive - no single unit can be a large fraction of the total. Storm damage is generated by a process where one event can exceed the sum of all others in the period.

items.stem: A clinic estimates next year's appointment demand by taking this year's number of patients and multiplying by the average number of visits per patient. Select every assumption this method requires.

options.text: Patient numbers will stay roughly stable
Visit frequency will not change
The clinic has enough staff to meet demand
No new clinic opens nearby
The average is not distorted by a small number of very frequent patients
Appointments are booked in advance
The clinic's records are digital

items.derivation: An assumption is required if the estimate fails when it fails. Staffing affects whether demand can be met, not what demand is. Option 5 is the subtle target - a mean visit rate carries no information if the distribution is skewed.

items.stem: An agricultural model predicts crop yield from rainfall. It was built on 12 years of data from one region, where irrigation was available throughout. Imagine other people want to use this model for agricultural prediction elsewhere. For each new setting, decide if the model holds, breaks, or you cannot tell from what you have been given

rows.text: The same region, after irrigation is removed
A neighbouring region with similar climate and irrigation
A region with double the rainfall range the model was built on

items.derivation: Irrigation is a condition the model was built under, so removing it changes the relationship. Doubling the rainfall range is extrapolation past observed data. The neighbouring region is genuinely undetermined.

items.stem: Mark every sentence that you think doesn't properly describe the underlying phenomenon.

options.text: Engagement fell 12% after the redesign.
Engagement punished the redesign.
The algorithm ranks posts by predicted watch time.
The algorithm decided it didn't like the post.
Regions with higher unemployment saw more business closures.
Unemployment is fighting back against the recovery.

items.derivation: The three targets assign intention or agency to a statistic or a function. Option 5 is a legitimate aggregate-level claim - an association between two measured quantities, no agency implied.

items.stem: You're head of strategy and sales in your company. A product's sign-up rate dropped 25%. There are three explanations: 1) A price rise took effect. 2) A new required onboarding verification step was launched. 3) It's a seasonal dip that occurs every year. What you know: the drop began within three days of the verification step. The price rise took effect five months earlier, with no visible effect at the time. Last year's data show a dip in this month, but of about 5%, not 25%. What are the most likely causes?Distribute 100 points across the three.

options.text: Pricing
Onboarding
Seasonality

items.derivation: Pricing is ruled out by a five-month gap with no effect. Seasonality accounts for roughly a fifth of the observed drop. Onboarding carries the remainder and matches the timing.

items.stem: Employees who use the company's internal wiki score 18% higher on performance reviews. You're asked to predict their performance this year.

parts.stem: You learn that an employee uses the wiki. How should you revise your estimate of their review score?

options.text: Up
Down
Unchanged

parts.stem: The company now makes wiki use mandatory for everyone. What happens to average review scores?

options.text: They rise
They fall
Little or no change

items.derivation: Wiki use marks an underlying disposition rather than conferring one. Observing it is informative. Mandating the behaviour does not distribute the disposition. The score is the DIFFERENCE between the two answers.

items.stem: Children who eat breakfast score higher on school tests. Select every factor consistent with the claim that breakfast is not the cause of the higher scores.

options.text: Households that provide breakfast may be more organized in general
Breakfast contains calories
Children who sleep badly may skip breakfast and also test worse
Families under financial strain may skip breakfast and face other disadvantages
The study included 4,000 children
Schools that serve breakfast may differ in other ways too
Tests are usually held in the morning

items.derivation: The four targets each describe a structure producing the association with breakfast doing nothing. Option 7 is the discriminating foil: morning testing describes a pathway THROUGH breakfast, which is a mechanism, not an alternative.

items.stem: In a hospital, wards that hold a daily safety briefing have fewer medication errors. The briefings were introduced one ward at a time over two years. The scheduling office set the order based on room availability, not on how many errors a ward had. In each ward, errors began to fall in the month after that ward's briefings started. Which explanation does this evidence best support?

options.text: Wards that already had fewer errors were given briefings first.
Both the briefings and the lower error rates come from better staffing on those wards.
The briefings reduce medication errors.
No causal direction can be established without a randomized trial.

items.derivation: Two facts do the work. The rollout order was set by room availability rather than by error counts, which rules out A. And errors fell in each ward in the month after that ward's own start date - a stable difference in staffing would not produce drops timed to each ward's individual start, which rules out B. D overstates: a staggered rollout with assignment unrelated to the outcome constrains direction well, even without randomization.

items.stem:
Suppose this is how things work (arrows denote a causal relation):

Drought → Low reservoir → Water restrictions

And separately:

Drought → Crop failure → Food price rise

Answer each question about this system.

rows.text: If the reservoir had been full, would there still have been water restrictions?
If the reservoir had been full, would the crops still have failed?
If there had been no drought, would food prices have risen?
If food prices had not risen, would there still have been a drought?

items.derivation: Read directly off the structure. No path from reservoir to crops, so changing the reservoir leaves crops alone. Food prices do not cause droughts. Rows 2 and 4 carry the diagnostic value.

items.stem: A bank finds that branches with a higher share of long-tenured loan officers have lower default rates. It concludes: assign long-tenured officers to our riskiest individual loans, and those loans will default less. Assume the data are accurate, the sample of branches is large, and the branch-level relationship is genuinely causal. What is still wrong with the conclusion?

options.text: Default rates are a lagging measure, so they may not reflect the quality of current lending decisions.
A branch's overall rate may come from factors no single officer controls, so it need not carry to individual loans.
Some third factor could be raising tenure and lowering defaults at the same time.
The number of branches studied may be too small to support a general claim.

items.derivation: An ecological inference. The stem stipulates away every distractor: A is a data-quality objection, excluded by 'the data are accurate'; C is confounding, excluded by 'genuinely causal'; D is sample size, excluded by 'the sample is large'. What survives is the level shift - a branch-level effect may run through caseload mix, supervision, or local underwriting norms, none of which transfer to a single officer on a single loan. Choosing A, C or D indicates reaching for a stock objection without reading the stipulations.

step1.stem: Of 500 people who completed a training programme, 340 said it improved their work. What is the chance the next person says the same?

step2.stem: You now meet someone who took the programme and describes, in vivid detail, how it wasted their time. What is your estimate now?

items.derivation: 340/500 = 68.0 percent. Adding one negative case: 340/501 = 67.9 percent. Correct movement is about one seventh of a percentage point. Typical drops are 10 to 20 points.

items.stem: A trial of 210 adults aged 40-65 with mild high blood pressure, at four clinics in one city, found a 12% improvement. What is the broadest group this result supports?

options.text: Just these 210 people
Adults aged 40-65 with mild high blood pressure in this city
Adults aged 40-65 with mild high blood pressure anywhere
Adults with high blood pressure generally
Adults generally

items.derivation: The sampling frame is four clinics in one city. Extending to anywhere requires a representativeness argument the study does not supply. Refusing to extend past the literal 210 participants discards the point of sampling.

items.stem: Research finding: people tend to reciprocate when given an unexpected favour. For each situation below, does this principle apply, or does it go beyond what the finding covers?

rows.text: Helping a colleague before you need anything from them
A company sending free samples to individual customers
One country lowering tariffs to prompt another to reciprocate
One department sending another department a report unprompted

items.derivation: The finding concerns individual psychology. Rows 1 and 2 involve individuals receiving something. A state is not a person and has no reciprocity intuition. Row 4 depends on whether individuals in the receiving department experience it personally - the item does not say.

step1.stem: Imagine an industry in which 12 out of every 100 suppliers of a product turn out to be unreliable. Your company hires a screening service to flag suppliers. It flags 85 out of every 100 unreliable suppliers, and also 15 out of every 100 reliable ones. Before any screening, what is the chance this supplier is unreliable?

step2.stem: The service has now flagged this supplier. What is the chance it is unreliable?

pole_rules.note: A U-dimension failure appearing in an E item. Record the flag; do not assign an E pole.

items.derivation: Prior odds 12:88 = 0.136. Likelihood ratio 85/15 = 5.667. Posterior odds 0.773, so P = 43.6 percent.

items.stem: You're a government official in charge of environmental policy. You must decide how to weigh different sources of information. The question you're facing: how fast a newly-introduced species will spread through a regional wetland. Four sources disagree. Distribute 100 points by how much weight each deserves.

options.text: An ecologist who specializes in invasive species in wetlands, publicly funded
A wildlife biologist with 25 years of experience in this region - working on mammals
A consultancy report commissioned by a developer, with fully documented methods
A science writer with an excellent record of correct predictions about technology

pole_rules.note: checked first: a flat allocation is false equivalence, and would otherwise match the option-4 rule below

items.derivation: Domain match dominates. Adjacent expertise carries real but reduced weight. An interested source with published methods is discountable but verifiable. Track record in an unrelated field transfers very little - this is the judgment the item tests.

items.stem: A newspaper's subscriptions rose 9% in the quarter it launched a podcast. Select every conclusion this evidence, on its own, establishes.

options.text: Subscriptions rose 9%
The podcast caused the rise
The podcast launched in a quarter when subscriptions rose
The podcast was worth what it cost
Without the podcast, subscriptions would have risen less
Something changed at the newspaper that quarter
Podcasts help newspapers

items.derivation: Options 1 and 3 restate what happened. Option 6 follows by definition. The rest require a comparison to what would have happened otherwise, which one quarter's figures cannot supply. Rejecting options 1 or 6 means 'be skeptical' has become a blanket policy.

items.stem: Some people argue that organizations should NOT use formal performance metrics. In 60-120 words, state the strongest version of that position - the one its ablest defender would give. Do not argue against it. Do not say whether you agree.
review_rubric: Fidelity: would a defender recognize this as their argument?
Strength: does it use the best reason, or the easiest one to knock down?
No caricature: no absurd premises, no imputed motives
Own view suppressed: no rebuttal smuggled in, no 'they claim that...'
strong_answer_markers: measures become targets and stop measuring what they measured
measurable work crowds out valuable unmeasurable work
measurement changes the behaviour it observes
gaming costs more than the information is worth
items.derivation: Not auto-scored in v1. Store responses for manual review.
